transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what's been going on that brought you in today?

Well… mostly it’s that I just cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. That’s the plainest way I can put it. I’m a carpenter, so there’s always noise and movement, and I used to be able to work through that, but now one saw starting up, somebody walking past the office, or even just a thought popping into my head about another job I’m supposed to look at, and I’m gone. I’ll be in the middle of something and suddenly I’m chasing that other thing in my head, or physically getting up to check something, and then I come back and I’ve lost where I was.

And it’s not just a little annoying anymore. It’s like the whole day gets away from me. I’ll start out thinking, okay, I’m going to focus on this one task, get it done, and then all these little interruptions pull me off course. By the end of the day I feel like I’ve been busy the whole time, but I can’t always point to what I actually finished. That’s really what brought me in.
Have you noticed that these difficulties with staying focused have been happening for most of your life, or is this something that started more recently?

No, it’s not brand new. I mean, it feels worse now because my work is more demanding and there’s more to juggle, but when I really think back, this goes way back.

Even in grade school, before I was 12, my teachers were always telling my mother the same sort of thing — that I was bright, but careless. That word came up a lot. I’d lose homework, or I’d do it and then somehow not turn it in, or I’d forget the instructions right after they were given. And I can remember sitting there supposed to be doing seatwork, and I’d just be staring out the window, watching a tree move or somebody on the playground or whatever, and then suddenly everyone else would be done and I’d barely started.

At the time I think people treated it like I just wasn’t trying hard enough, or I was being lazy or sloppy, but it didn’t feel like that to me. It was more like my mind would just slip off without me noticing. So, no, I wouldn’t say it started recently. It’s been there most of my life, just maybe more obvious now.
As you were growing up, did you also find yourself moving around a lot, having trouble sitting still, or acting without thinking — like blurting things out or interrupting others?

Yeah… I mean, not so much like I was the kid bouncing off the walls, at least not how I remember it. But the sitting still part, that’s definitely there, and it still is.

Like if I have to sit at the desk and do estimates, that’s one of the worst things for me. I’ll be sitting there with the papers or the computer in front of me, and I know I need to just stay there and finish it, but inside I feel all wound up. It’s not even that my body can’t sit there exactly — it’s more like there’s this pressure building, like I need to get up and move around or go check something in the shop or walk outside for a minute. And the longer I try to force myself to stay put, the more agitated I feel.

Same with long meetings. I can sit there, but I’m uncomfortable the whole time. I’ll be thinking, “Just stay here, just get through it,” but inside I’m itching to move. And it’s not because of my wrist or anything now — that’s healed. So I can’t really blame it on that. It’s just this restless feeling, like my body wants to be doing something even when I know I’m supposed to stay seated and finish what’s in front of me.
